title: Stateful Stream Processing
summary: Aggregations, joins, and dedup all need to remember something across events that never fully arrive. State is what makes that possible — and checkpointing is what keeps it alive across a crash.

slides.markdown:
A per-event filter ("drop events where amount < 0") needs nothing but the current event. A running count, a join, or a dedup check needs to remember *something* about events it saw earlier — and "earlier" can mean seconds or hours ago, across a process that might crash in between.

That memory is **state**, and it's the piece that turns a stateless per-event pipeline into the aggregations and joins covered in the last two topics. This topic covers how state is stored, how it survives a crash via checkpointing, and the two production failure modes that follow directly from getting state wrong: unbounded growth, and losing it on recovery.

slides.sectionTitle: Why aggregation, joins, and dedup all need state
slides.markdown:
Three operations that look different on the surface share the same requirement underneath:

- **Aggregation** (a running count or sum for a window) needs to remember the running total so far — each new event updates it rather than recomputing from scratch.
- **Stream-stream joins** need to remember events from one side of the join while waiting for a matching event on the other side, since they rarely arrive at the same instant.
- **Deduplication** needs to remember which event IDs it's already seen, so a retried or redelivered event can be recognized and dropped.

In all three, the correct output for the *current* event depends on information from *previous* events. A purely stateless processor — one that only ever looks at the event in front of it — cannot do any of the three. State is the mechanism that lets "now" depend on "before."

slides.sectionTitle: A state store backing an aggregation
slides.markdown:
Picture a running aggregation as three parts working together: incoming events update a **state store** (the running total for each key), the engine periodically writes a **checkpoint** — a durable snapshot of that store — to persistent storage, and on a crash the engine reloads the most recent checkpoint and resumes from there instead of starting over.

slides.subTitle: Snapshotting state so a crash doesn't mean starting over
slides.markdown:
**Checkpointing** is the periodic act of durably saving a consistent snapshot of all state, along with the position (offset) in each input source that snapshot corresponds to. On a crash, the engine restores state from the last checkpoint and resumes reading from the recorded offset, rather than reprocessing the entire stream from the beginning.

The checkpoint interval is a direct trade-off: checkpointing every 10 seconds means a crash loses at most 10 seconds of state and has to reprocess only that much — but checkpointing itself has overhead (pausing or slowing processing briefly to take a consistent snapshot), so checkpointing too frequently can measurably hurt steady-state throughput.

Without checkpointing, a stateful job's only recovery option is a full restart from the beginning of retained data — for a job with hours of accumulated state, that can mean hours of reprocessing before it's caught back up to real time.

Where the live state actually lives (before it's checkpointed) is itself a choice with a clear trade-off:

| | In-memory backend | Disk-backed backend |
|---|---|---|
| Read/write speed | Fastest — no serialization or disk I/O per access | Slower — every access serializes to/from disk |
| Max state size | Bounded by available RAM per worker | Bounded by disk, typically far larger |
| Checkpoint cost | Must copy all state out on every checkpoint | Can checkpoint incrementally, since data is already on disk |

An in-memory backend is the right default when state per key is small and total state fits comfortably in RAM — most windowed aggregations. A disk-backed backend (commonly an embedded key-value store like RocksDB) becomes necessary once state grows past what memory can hold — large join buffers, long-retention deduplication sets, or high-cardinality per-key state — accepting slower per-access latency in exchange for scale.

slides.sectionTitle: Stream-stream joins need bounded state on both sides
slides.markdown:
Joining two streams — say, ad impressions with the clicks that followed them — means buffering events from each side while waiting for a match from the other, since matching events almost never arrive simultaneously.

Critically, that buffer has to be **time-bounded**. If an impression's matching click can arrive anywhere from 0 seconds to 3 days later, the join has to keep every unmatched impression in state for up to 3 days before giving up on it — and every one of those 3 days' worth of impressions sits in state simultaneously, at whatever the impression rate is.

This is why stream-stream joins are typically specified with an explicit **join window** ("match within 1 hour") rather than an unbounded "eventually." The join window isn't just a business decision about relevance — it's the number that determines how much state the join needs to hold at any given time.

A join or a deduplication check implemented with no expiry keeps every key it's ever seen, forever. State grows monotonically with total historical volume, not with current traffic — a dedup set that's been running for a year holds a year's worth of IDs, even though only the last few minutes of them are ever actually useful for catching a real duplicate.

This fails slowly and then all at once: state grows for weeks without incident, checkpoints get gradually larger and slower to write, memory or disk pressure creeps up — and then a checkpoint fails outright, or the job runs out of memory, usually during a traffic spike that's the worst possible time for it to happen.

The fix is always the same shape: give state an expiry. A dedup set only needs to remember IDs for as long as a duplicate could plausibly arrive; a join buffer only needs to hold unmatched events for as long as the join window. Unbounded state is very rarely an intentional design choice — it's almost always a missing TTL.

Recovering from a crash needs two pieces of information together, not one: the **state snapshot** (what the aggregation, join, or dedup set looked like) and the **source offset** that snapshot corresponds to (exactly where in the input to resume reading from).

If these two get out of sync — say, the offset was committed slightly after the state was checkpointed — recovery either reprocesses a handful of events the state already accounted for (producing double-counted results) or skips events the state hasn't seen yet (producing gaps). Correct checkpointing takes a **consistent** snapshot of both together, atomically, which is exactly what the exactly-once semantics topic later in this group is built on.

The practical takeaway: "we checkpoint state" is an incomplete design unless it also specifies how that checkpoint stays consistent with the offsets committed against each source.

slides.sectionTitle: State TTL as a required design decision
slides.markdown:
Every piece of stateful logic should have an explicit answer to "how long does this state need to live," decided at design time — not discovered later when a checkpoint starts failing.

Some concrete numbers to anchor this: a dedup set for retried API calls might only need a **few minutes** of TTL, since retries happen quickly or not at all. A join buffer matching impressions to clicks might need **hours**. A session window (from the previous topic) needs state for exactly as long as sessions stay open, which is itself bounded by the session gap timeout.

Treating TTL as an afterthought — "we'll add expiry once we see a problem" — means the problem you'll see is a production incident, at whatever scale the state happened to reach by then. Treating it as a day-one design question means picking a number once, with the business logic still fresh, rather than reverse-engineering the right TTL from an outage.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers on state and checkpoints
slides.markdown:
To make the trade-offs concrete: a deduplication set holding a 24-hour TTL at 10,000 events/second, with a 16-byte key, is on the order of **10,000 × 86,400 × 16 bytes ≈ 14 GB** of raw key data before any per-key overhead from the storage engine — clearly past what you'd want resident purely in one worker's memory, and a strong signal to reach for a disk-backed backend.

Checkpoint intervals in production commonly sit in the **10-second to 1-minute range** — frequent enough that a crash loses at most that much reprocessing time, infrequent enough that the checkpoint's own I/O overhead stays a small fraction of steady-state processing.

These aren't universal constants — they depend entirely on your key size, TTL, and event rate — but doing this arithmetic once for your actual workload is what turns "we should probably use RocksDB" from a guess into a decision with a number behind it.

State and checkpointing are the mechanism; the guarantee you can actually claim on top of them is a separate question. The next topic, Exactly-Once Semantics, covers exactly that: how a consistent state-plus-offset checkpoint combines with idempotent or transactional sinks to produce an end-to-end guarantee — and why "exactly-once" is a much stronger and more expensive claim than "we checkpoint state," even though the two are often conflated.

Carry forward one framing from this topic: every stateful operator has a size, and that size is a design decision (TTL, join window, backend choice), never an emergent property you discover from an incident.
